doc.title: Phoebe Jacobs and Jackie Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006

title: Donald Harrison, Kidd Jordan and the avant-garde of the 1960s
summary: Harris recounts Harrison's avant-garde past and talks about the Coltrane and Miles years as expressing civil rights frustration.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Exactly. You just, you can’t tell. And then even Donald as he gave me this smooth jazz album, we talked about how he played because Kidd was his teacher, how for a period of time he only wanted to play avante garde. You know, now people don’t know that and even the music that he records now you would have to dig way back to find an avante garde album of Donald Harrison if it really exists, and I didn’t know he had played avante garde but he did. He says, “Oh for a minute I was mad too when I played that.”
No, no, no, not mad, well you see —

Well yes, angry. But you see and we talked about, we had a great conversation because we talked about the Coltrane years. And the Miles years. And Kidd. And the artists of that time. I mean this is during the civil rights movement in the sixties. And so these artists were expressing their feeling of frustration and also they were actually expressing the feelings of the African-American community in America at that time and they were taking us from one part of our history and how we were living to the next part of history. And so that is what that music was all about. And you know different groups were formed, you know, out of this. And so, and then that art of that genre of music, I attended the Vision Music Festival, and then I was thinking there’s not a whole lot of young musicians playing that music. And so now I think and I says I hope this is not a dying art.
